query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin NiCr transition interlayer between a copper substrate and a wear‐resistant high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating will enhance metallurgical bonding, reduce thermal and stress mismatches, and thereby improve adhesion and wear performance of the overall composite system.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper (Cu) matrix in its as-received condition with native surface properties requiring improved wear resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin engineered NiCr interlayer onto the Cu substrate followed by application of a wear‐resistant high-entropy alloy coating.
generation.conditions: Testing under wear, repeated frictional contact, and elevated temperature conditions typical of surface protection applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The NiCr interlayer serves as a graded interface that chemically and mechanically bonds the Cu substrate to the HEA coating.
generation.mechanism: The NiCr interlayer improves metallurgical compatibility by reducing thermal expansion and mechanical property mismatches between the Cu matrix and the HEA coating, thereby minimizing delamination risks and local stress concentrations under wear conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite system with the NiCr interlayer will exhibit superior adhesion, resulting in enhanced wear resistance and surface protection compared to a system with direct HEA deposition on Cu.
generation.baseline: A Cu substrate coated directly with a HEA without an engineered interlayer, which historically shows issues with adhesion and delamination due to mismatched thermophysical properties.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the interlayer is contingent on its optimal thickness and processing conditions; extreme operational temperatures or environments may still challenge the interlayer’s ability to mitigate mismatches.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of adhesion and wear resistance improvement is uncertain and will need to be quantified experimentally, particularly under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with a Cu substrate directly coated with a wear‐resistant HEA and the other with a Cu substrate first coated with a thin NiCr interlayer followed by the same HEA coating. Subject both sets to identical wear and friction tests at elevated temperatures.
measurements: Adhesion strength via scratch testing or peel tests
Wear resistance using standardized friction and abrasion tests
Microstructural characterization of the coating–substrate interface (e.g., SEM, EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the NiCr interlayer do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in adhesion strength and wear resistance over the directly coated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

frame.limitation: Choosing an adherent coating that is both wear resistant and metallurgically compatible with Cu; issues such as poor bonding or mismatched thermophysical properties have limited previous approaches.
